readerTitle: Three ways to find a plumber, and what they teach about marketing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소업체, 소규모 IT 지원 회사) · 일상 장면 (배관공 찾기)
insight: 마케팅 채널은 '내가 얼마나 통제하나'와 '고객이 얼마나 믿어주나'를 맞바꾸는 선택이며, 유료·자체·획득 미디어는 서로 경쟁하기보다 서로를 키운다.
misconception: 마케팅은 곧 광고비다. 돈을 더 쓰면 손님이 더 온다. 입소문은 공짜다.

sources.text: 마케팅 업계에서 널리 쓰이는 분류 (paid, owned, earned media)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 유료·자체·획득 미디어 분류는 2000년대 후반부터 업계에서 널리 쓰였습니다. 특정 인물이나 회사가 만들었다고 카드에 적지 않았습니다. 기원을 추가하려면 1차 자료를 먼저 확인하세요.
청소업체의 월 $1,000 예산과 광고 중단 후 문의 감소는 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.
Watch out 카드의 '돈을 받은 추천은 밝혀야 한다는 규정이 많은 곳에 있다'는 일반적 서술입니다. 특정 국가의 법 조항은 다루지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Three ways to find a plumber
body: It's Saturday and your sink is leaking. You find a plumber three ways.
A neighbor texts you a name. A search page shows a plumber marked *Sponsored* at the top. A third plumber has a website full of clear prices and before-and-after photos.
Most people call the neighbor's plumber first. That choice says a lot about how marketing works.

image.label: A phone showing a neighbor's text, a sponsored result and a plumber's website
image.brief: 새는 싱크대 앞에서 스마트폰을 든 사람. 화면 위로 말풍선 세 개: 이웃의 문자 메시지, "Sponsored" 표시가 붙은 검색 결과, 배관공 웹사이트. 이웃 문자 말풍선이 가장 밝게 빛남. 실제 검색엔진·앱 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The calls stopped when the ads did.
body: Maria runs a house-cleaning business. She spends $1,000 a month on search ads. Last month she paused them, and new calls nearly stopped.
What should she do with next month's $1,000?

options.text: Put it all back into ads, maybe more
options.feedback: Ads bring calls quickly and she controls them. But she rents attention month by month, and nothing builds up for later.

options.text: Keep some ads, and spend the rest on a better website and making referrals easy
options.feedback: She keeps calls coming while building assets that keep working when she stops paying. Results from the website and referrals arrive more slowly.

options.text: Drop ads and rely on word of mouth
options.feedback: Recommendations are trusted, but she can't switch them on. Without ads, she may not have enough new customers to talk about her.

cards.title: Not all customers arrived the same way.
body: Maria sorted her customers by how they found her. Ad customers came fast but compared prices hard. Referred customers booked quickly and rarely haggled.
A few found her through her own site and email newsletter. Those people already knew her prices and photos before they called.
Three routes, three different kinds of attention.

cards.title: Earned, owned and paid
body: **Paid** attention is what you buy: ads, sponsored posts, flyers. **Owned** is what you run yourself: your website, shop sign, van, email list. **Earned** is what others say about you: referrals, reviews, press.
Most businesses use all three. The skill is knowing what each one is good for.

image.label: Three circles: Paid, Owned, Earned
image.brief: 겹치는 원 세 개 인포그래픽. "Paid"(광고판, 동전 아이콘), "Owned"(웹사이트, 가게 간판, 업무용 밴), "Earned"(말풍선, 별점). 원이 겹치는 부분에 작은 화살표로 서로 연결됨. 실제 플랫폼 로고 금지.

cards.title: Control and trust pull in opposite directions.
body: Each type trades control for credibility.
list: **Paid:** you choose the message and timing. You pay every time, and people discount ads.
**Owned:** you control it and build it once. It only reaches people who already found you.
**Earned:** the most trusted. You can't buy it or control what gets said.
cards.callout: The more you control a message, the less people tend to believe it.

cards.title: The three feed each other.
body: Paid brings in first customers. Good work turns some of them into referrals and reviews. Owned channels, like an email list, let you reach those customers again without paying twice.
So a strong ad that lands on a weak website wastes money. And glowing reviews help more when your site shows them.
cards.softwareNote: A software company might buy ads for a free trial (paid), teach through its help guides and onboarding emails (owned), and win reviews and users' posts (earned). Trials from referrals often convert better because the trust came first.

cards.title: Earned is not free.
body: Referrals cost you through quality, time and sometimes a thank-you discount. A business with no customers yet has no one to talk about it, so paid often has to come first.

Faking earned attention backfires. Bought reviews or paid endorsements dressed up as honest opinions are just hidden ads. Many places require paid promotion to be disclosed, and customers stop trusting you when they find out.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You run a three-person firm that handles computers and networks for small offices. You want more law-firm clients. Hiring an IT firm feels risky to them, because a mistake could expose client files.

options.text: Run online ads aimed at law-office managers
options.feedback: Ads put you in front of the right people fast. But for a risky purchase, an ad alone rarely earns enough trust to win the call.

options.text: Write a case study with a happy law-firm client and ask them for two introductions
options.feedback: The case study is owned and keeps working. The introductions are earned and carry a peer's trust. It's slower than ads, and depends on that client saying yes.

options.text: Book a large booth at a big general business expo
options.feedback: You pay for wide reach, but most visitors aren't law firms. The money buys attention you mostly don't need.

cards.title: Rent attention, build attention, earn attention.
body: Paid gets you seen now. Owned keeps working after you stop paying. Earned is what people trust most. Plan for all three, and let each feed the next.
**Try it today:** list where your last ten customers came from. Mark each one paid, owned or earned. Which column is empty?
